This measurement was derived from a large series of hatchlings emerging from eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions. Following eclosion, these young individuals begin a phase of rapid somatic growth, gradually progressing through the juvenile stage. The timing of sexual maturation, however, is strongly modulated by environmental temperature. When maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], which approximates the average thermal conditions in their native habitat, females attain puberty considerably later than males. Specifically, the time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 274.5 days [tp = approximately 274.5 days], a duration nearly two months longer than that observed in their male counterpar at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]ts. This delay in female maturation is likely linked to the greater energetic investment required for vitellogenesis and the production of yolk-laden eggs, a common pattern among small-bodied oviparous reptiles.

Males of Anolis nebulosus, in contrast, follow a slightly accelerated developmental trajectory. Under the same thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], male Clouded Anoles reach sexual maturity at roughly 213.5 days after hatching [tp = roughly 213.5 days after hatching], representing a time since birth at puberty that is about 61 days shorter than in females. This earlier onset of gonadal activation in males is a widespread life-history strategy among anoles, permitting young males to begin establishing territories and competing for access to gravid females before they have completed their full somatic growth. The snout-vent length at puberty for males is 3.5 cm [Lp = 3.5 cm], a body size that is noticeably smaller than the 3.7 cm [Lp = 3.7 cm] required for the initiation of reproductive activity in females. This size dimorphism in maturation thresholds reflects the differing selective pressures on each sex: males can afford to begin reproducing at a smaller body size, whereas females must achieve a larger structural size to accommodate the physical demands of egg production and successful nesting.

The ultimate body sizes achieved by adult Clouded Anoles further illustrate the species’ life-history trade-offs. Females, which invest heavily in egg production, continue to grow after reaching puberty and attain a maximum snout-vent length of 5.28 cm [Li = 5.28 cm]. Males, by comparison, are characterized by a slightly smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 4.65 cm [Li = 4.65 cm], a pattern of female-biased size dimorphism that is relatively common among anoles and is often attributed to fecundity selection favoring larger body cavities in females. In terms of mass, the ultimate wet weight recorded for adult Clouded Anoles is 1.77 grams [Wwi = 1.77 grams], a value derived from size-corrected allometric equations based on lacertid lizards. This modest adult mass, combined with the species’ short stature, classifies Anolis nebulosus as a relatively small member of its genus, with life-history characteristics that are closely tied to its arboreal, insectivorous lifestyle in the seasonally dry forests of western Mexico.

Reproductive output in this species is tightly linked to temperature, with the maximum reproductive rate being achieved under optimal thermal conditions. At a constant ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females are capable of producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with up to twelve clutches deposited annually [F_R_i = up to twelve clutches deposited annually]. This high annual fecundity is characteristic of many tropical and subtropical anoles, which exploit extended breeding seasons to offset the relatively low survival rates of eggs and hatchlings. Each egg, once fertilized through cloacal copulation, undergoes a developmental period that is dependent on incubation temperature. Under the shared thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the species also exhibits its maximum lifespan, with the oldest individuals recorded at approximately 730 days [am = approximately 730 days]. This relatively short lifespan, spanning just two years under ideal captive conditions, underscores the species’ reliance on high annual reproductive output as a compensatory strategy for high early-life mortality.

Comparative physiological studies of Anolis nebulosus have highlighted the role of temperature in shaping its life-history pace. The maximum lifespan of 730 days [am = 730 days], measured at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is typical for small-bodied anoles that inhabit environments with moderate thermal variability. In contrast to longer-lived congeners from cooler, more stable habitats, the Clouded Anole’s short lifespan is coupled with an early and intense reproductive schedule. The observed female age at puberty of 274.5 days since birth [tp = 274.5 days since birth] and the male age at puberty of 213.5 days since birth [tp = 213.5 days since birth], both recorded at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], fall within the range reported for other Mexican anole species with comparable body sizes. Field studies in the species’ native thorn-scrub habitat of Jalisco suggest that these thermal conditions are rarely sustained year-round, meaning that wild individuals likely experience slower developmental rates and lower total fecundity than those maintained under constant optimal temperatures in the laboratory, a discrepancy that underscores the importance of microhabitat selection in determining life-history outcomes.
